newsitem.title: GERMANY: German law reform to put people before property.
newsitem.headline: German law reform to put people before property.

text.p: Germany plans a major reform of its 125-year-old criminal laws to punish violent acts like rape or attempted kidnapping more than crimes against property such as robbery, Bonn's justice minister said on Friday.
The reform would correct a fundamental imbalance in the laws dating back to 1871, when people were less threatened by physical violence than now, Edzard Schmidt-Jortzig said.

"We want tougher punishment against causing bodily harm," Schmidt-Jortzig told RTL television. "It doesn't fit into today's legal thinking that this should not be protected the same way as valuable objects are."
Liberal jurists have long demanded a reform, arguing that the legal bias towards property was cynical in a country whose constitution proclaims: "Human dignity is unassailable."

This imbalance caused an international outcry in 1993 when a man who stabbed U.S. tennis star Monica Seles at a match in Hamburg received only a two-year suspended sentence in court because the judge saw no proof he had wanted to kill her.
The reform would boost the maximum punishment for sexual abuse of children from 10 to 15 years and double top penalties for inflicting serious bodily harm from five to 10 years.
It would also make a bid to kidnap or inflict bodily harm a crime, just like attempted robbery or murder. Seles' attacker might have been jailed if attempting to injure were a crime.

"Current law leads to the unacceptable paradox that the attempted theft of a pram is a crime but the bid to kidnap the infant lying in it is not," remarked Munich's Sueddeutsche Zeitung in a story revealing the reform plan.

Stiffer punishments for sex offences -- now a high-profile crime in Germany following revelations of child abuse in neighbouring Belgium and the murder of a seven-year-old girl by a sex killer in Bavaria -- should remove other inconsistencies in the law, a ministry spokeswoman said.

Under the current law, the maximum sentence for sexually abusing a child is five years, equal to the normal penalty for purse-snatching. The minimum sentence for killing a woman while raping her is the same as for robbing a bank with a toy pistol.

The reform, now being circulated in draft form among government ministries for their comments, would also reduce some penalties for crimes against property to bring them into line with the new approach.
The draft would lower minimum penalties for serious robbery from five to two years -- an idea that provoked criticism from the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU).
Schmidt-Jortzig's liberal Free Democrats (FDP) and the CSU are allies in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition.
West Germany last attempted a major overhaul of its criminal laws in the 1970s, but the bid got bogged down in parliament.

German courts were strongly criticised in the early 1990s for soft sentences on racist firebombers, but most of these were youths tried under juvenile laws strongly based on the principle of rehabilitation rather than retribution.
Jurists preparing the draft, which is not expected to be submitted to parliament until next year, came across several anomalies while combing the books for outdated laws.
The stiffest punishment for burning a field of crops is 10 years in jail, for example, while setting fire to crops already stored in a depot would only carry a two-year maximum sentence.
